extracted.intended_audience: secondary mathematics teachers, curriculum developers, and mathematics education reformers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for organizing high school mathematics curriculum around the cognitive 'habits of mind' mathematicians use, detailing specific student habits and mathematical approaches that curricula should develop. Intended to inform teachers and curriculum developers about what ways of thinking to cultivate and how to structure learning experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value habits of mind over specific content
rubrics_metrics.description: Curriculum should elevate the methods by which mathematics is created to equal status with established results; prioritize developing students' mathematical habits over teaching a particular bag of facts or fashionable topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design courses to help students become comfortable with ill-posed problems, abstraction, conjecturing, experimenting, and inventing. Examples: prefer approaches (difference equations, linear algebra, combinatorics) that cultivate algorithmic and structural thinking rather than transient topical fads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comfort with ill-posed and fuzzy problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should be comfortable with problems that are not fully specified or that have 'fuzzy' requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage false starts, work on special cases, suspend details (e.g., lemmas without proofs) to see whether assumptions help, and treat such problems as opportunities for conjecture and modeling rather than failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop general habits of mind used by mathematicians
rubrics_metrics.description: Every course should be used to help students develop general cognitive habits (pattern detection, experimentation, abstraction, etc.) shared across disciplines, not just domain-specific facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These habits are relearned in domains and require explicit curricular emphasis; curricula should build a repertoire of heuristics and the judgment of when to use them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Students should be pattern sniffers
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate a delight in finding hidden regularities and shortcuts in numerical or structural data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have students search for patterns in tables (e.g., squares 1–100), in calculations (arithmetic series), and in posed problems (e.g., which primes are sums of two squares). Encourage generating conjectures like divisibility tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Students should be experimenters
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should habitually perform experiments (including thought experiments) as a central technique in mathematical inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach recording results, keeping variables fixed, trying extreme/small cases, varying parameters methodically. Also teach healthy skepticism about empirical results and limitations of experimental methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Students should be describers
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should develop skill in creating precise descriptions and communicating mathematical ideas (invent notation, argue, write).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect students to: give precise step-by-step descriptions, invent useful notation when ordinary language is cumbersome, present convincing arguments or proofs to peers, and write polished notes of their investigations for others. Foster classroom culture of collaboration and critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Students should be tinkerers
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should habitually take mathematical ideas apart and reassemble them to see effects of modifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage experimenting with changing the order of operations (e.g., rotation then translation vs translation then rotation), omitting pieces, or altering definitions; use 'mistakes' as starting points for inquiry (ask what fractions satisfy a false identity, or define operations that would make it true).

rubrics_metrics.name: Students should be inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should invent mathematical objects, rules, algorithms, or axioms motivated by situations rather than arbitrary creation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame invention as modeling: axioms/systems should arise to bring clarity to phenomena (example: inventing the operation a ⊕ b = (a + 2b)/3 from bargaining process). Encourage seeking isomorphisms between structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Students should look for isomorphisms (structural parallels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Habit of seeking different instances of the same mathematical structure so students see analogies across contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage mapping operations across domains (e.g., union of sets analogous to sum of numbers) and using these analogies to transfer insight and build abstractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Students should be visualizers
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop multiple kinds of visualization skills: mental imagery of spatial objects, visual analogues for non-visual ideas, and visual accompaniments to symbolic processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach subskills: reasoning about plane/3D subsets with/without drawings; visualizing data via tables/graphs; visualizing relationships (Venn diagrams, factor trees); visualizing processes (machines, input-output); visualizing change (continuous variation); visualizing calculations (mental arithmetic imagery, factoring an integer). Use area models for algebraic identities as examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Students should be conjecturers
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should habitually form plausible conjectures based on experimentation, experience, and understanding of underlying algorithms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage data-driven conjectures but push for deeper grounding (combine anecdotal evidence, prior experience, and algorithmic analysis). Use examples where naive conjectures fail to motivate analysis (Logo procedure examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Students should be guessers (use educated guesses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage starting from plausible solutions and working backwards; checking guesses to gain familiarity and new insights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat guessing as a research strategy; use it to get traction on hard problems and to iterate toward closer approximations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematicians talk big and think small (translate to special cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate the habit of translating general statements into special, concrete cases to build intuition and spot counterexamples or essential structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep a repertoire of concrete examples; begin with problems and examples from which general theories emerge (e.g., mapping 3D into 2D matrices intuition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematicians talk small and think big (extract deep theory from simple problems)
rubrics_metrics.description: Train students to see how simple problems can motivate deep theories and how sophisticated theories often solve easy-to-state problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use elementary puzzles (sum of two squares, Fermat's problem origins) to show emergence of large theories; encourage abstraction from simple cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematicians use functions (three uses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasize studying change mechanisms (functions) across three roles: algorithms (transformations), dependences (analytic/causal relationships), and mappings (combinatorial correspondences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have students define functions on geometric objects, create translator functions between viewpoints, and use algorithmic, analytic, and combinatorial perspectives in problem solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple points of view
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should learn to analyze objects from several mathematical perspectives (algebraic, analytic, arithmetic, geometric) and use their interplay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give tasks that require switching viewpoints (e.g., complex numbers via algebra, geometry, arithmetic, analysis) and value synthesis of methods (Gauss examples, Soifer's book).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mix deduction and experiment (role of proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate both experimental investigation and deductive proof, using each as research techniques rather than treating proof as an after-the-fact ritual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame proofs as connection-making and explanation that arise during investigation; show how proofs suggest new theorems and sharpen results (examples: cake-cutting problem, proofs that evolve with construction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Push the language (extend and invent mathematical language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage extending definitions and notational systems to apply familiar rules in new cases and to create objects that behave as desired (assume existence to explore consequences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples like extending exponent rules, negative row interpretations in Pascal's triangle, or assuming entities to derive contradictions/proofs (fundamental theorem of algebra).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use intellectual chants (mental rehearsal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge and cultivate the meditative rehearsal mathematicians use: alternating between scribbling and reflective rehashing to spot subtle connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include in materials ruminations and reflective writeups of problem-solving processes; have students record and reflect on how they approached problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometers use proportional reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach geometric thinking that emphasizes ratios and proportional relationships as primary quantities (visualize products/quotients of lengths, constant ratios).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use computer tools to build intuition (measure boxes, dilations), and link proportional reasoning to vector methods and fractal geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometers use several languages at once
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage using multiple representational languages in geometry (turtle geometry, vectors, analytic coordinates, algebraic languages) within single investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design problems where students translate between languages and harness multiple tools to solve geometric problems; this supports 'multiple points of view' habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometers use geometric language broadly (one language for everything)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach students to recast non-geometric problems in geometric terms (points, lines, hyperplanes) to gain coherence and new insights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show examples like representing integer solutions as points on hyperplanes and extending geometric notions (triangle, angle sums) to abstract coordinate settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometers love systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate appreciation of whole structured systems in geometry and tendency to build coherent systems that interrelate concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage creating and exploring self-contained geometric systems and hobby-like explorations that reveal systemic properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraists use abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage abstracting similarities between systems (capture shared algorithms/properties) to create new algebraic structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples comparing integers and polynomials, roots of unity leading to modular exponent arithmetic, and show how abstraction lets one 'calculate with exponents' rather than base objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraists like algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach design and analysis of algorithms as central algebraic habit: recipes for calculations, recursively defined procedures, and methods that reveal structural properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide algorithmic tasks (Euclidean algorithm for gcd and coefficients; resultant matrix for common roots; ψ-operator for counting lock combinations) and emphasize inductive/recursive definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraists break things into parts (decomposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Train students to identify building blocks (e.g., prime factorization) and structural decomposition theorems to analyze and extend results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use structure theorems (fundamental theorem of arithmetic, decomposition of vector spaces, finite abelian groups) and equivalence-class partitions (integers mod n) as examples of the technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraists extend systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach habit of enlarging a system (extensions) to see how properties change and to discover new structure (e.g., integers → Gaussian integers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explore how primes factor differently under extension, and show how extension reveals criteria (e.g., primes mod 4) and leads to deep theories (class field theory, Galois).

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraists represent things (use representations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Promote representing less-understood objects via mappings to well-understood structures (e.g., points ↔ R^2, linear maps ↔ matrices) to study interplay and gain insights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight analytic geometry, linear algebra matrix representations, and group representations as central methods; give tasks making representations explicit and useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate calculations with invented objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach students to perform calculations not only with numbers but with objects invented for purposes (permutations, transformations) and to treat them as systems to study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete puzzles (card-shuffle permutation example) to show how permutations become mathematical objects (cycle graphs, T^12 = identity), and then abstract to study their algebraic properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop habit of writing and collaborative critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should write up thoughts, proofs, conjectures, and reflections and participate in peer critique to refine arguments and habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate regular writing and revision tasks, encourage presentation to classmates, and build classroom culture of collaborative questioning and feedback.
